pa-peds-geri-l01.q: A 9-month-old cannot yet sit without support and is not crawling. What is the correct response?
choices: Reassure and recheck at the next well visit, since crawling varies widely
Refer for developmental evaluation now, since sitting alone by 9 months is an anchor and this infant has missed it
Order an MRI immediately without further exam
Diagnose cerebral palsy on this finding alone
pa-peds-geri-l01.why: Sitting alone by 9 months is a referral deadline; missing it warrants evaluation, not reassurance. Imaging and a cerebral palsy diagnosis both require more workup than a single missed milestone provides.

pa-peds-geri-l01.q: A father asks when it becomes clear which hand his 10-month-old prefers. What should you tell him?
choices: Hand preference before 12 to 18 months is normal and expected
Hand preference this early is a red flag for possible hemiparesis and warrants attention
Hand preference only matters after age 5
Hand preference always indicates left-handedness genetically
pa-peds-geri-l01.why: A clear hand preference before 12 to 18 months is atypical and can signal weakness on the non-preferred side (hemiparesis). It is not simply an early sign of handedness, and waiting until age 5 to care about it would delay recognition of a treatable problem.

pa-peds-geri-l02.q: Why is blood pressure a poor early indicator of shock in children?
choices: Children have naturally high vascular resistance that masks hypotension
Strong compensatory vasoconstriction and tachycardia keep blood pressure normal until a large volume has been lost
Pediatric blood pressure cuffs are inaccurate
Children cannot mount a tachycardic response
pa-peds-geri-l02.why: Children compensate with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, keeping blood pressure normal until roughly 30 to 40 percent of volume is lost, so a normal pressure is falsely reassuring. Cuff inaccuracy and absent tachycardia are not the mechanism.

pa-peds-geri-l02.q: What is the fastest, most reliable way to estimate a sick child's weight when a scale is not immediately available?
choices: Ask the parent's best guess only, since formulas are unreliable
Use a length-based color-coded resuscitation tape, or the age-based formula, then confirm in kilograms as soon as possible
Estimate weight in pounds since kilograms are rarely used in pediatrics
Delay all weight-based dosing until an exact scale weight is obtained
pa-peds-geri-l02.why: A length-based tape or the (age x 2) + 8 formula gives a fast, adequate estimate for emergent dosing; exact weight can follow once feasible. Pounds are not the standard unit for pediatric dosing, and waiting for a precise weight would delay time-critical treatment.

pa-peds-geri-l03.q: Why is a bagged urine specimen unacceptable for diagnosing UTI in a febrile infant?
choices: Bagged specimens are painful to collect
Bagged specimens are frequently contaminated by skin and perineal flora, producing false-positive cultures
Bagged specimens cannot be refrigerated
Bagged specimens require too large a volume
pa-peds-geri-l03.why: Skin flora contaminate bag specimens so often that a positive culture cannot be trusted, which is why catheterization or suprapubic aspiration is required. Pain, refrigeration, and volume are not the reasons bag specimens are rejected.

pa-peds-geri-l03.q: What distinguishes a complex febrile seizure from a simple one?
choices: Any seizure occurring with a temperature above 39 C
Focal features, duration over 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours
Seizure occurring in a child older than 5 years only
Any seizure that stops on its own
pa-peds-geri-l03.why: Focality, prolonged duration, or more than one seizure in 24 hours defines complex febrile seizure and changes the workup. Temperature height, self-terminating seizures, and age alone do not define complexity.

pa-peds-geri-l04.q: Why are bronchodilators not routinely given for bronchiolitis?
choices: They are too expensive for routine use
Trials show no consistent improvement in oxygenation, admission rate, or length of stay for the average infant
They are contraindicated under 2 years of age
They worsen RSV replication
pa-peds-geri-l04.why: Bronchiolitis is viral, small-airway inflammation and mucus plugging rather than bronchospasm, so bronchodilators show no consistent benefit in trials. Cost and viral replication are not the stated rationale, and they are not formally contraindicated, just not routinely effective.

pa-peds-geri-l04.q: What is the concern with using magnesium in a severe pediatric asthma exacerbation, and how is it managed?
choices: It should never be given to children under any circumstance
It can cause hypotension, so it is given as a slow IV infusion with monitoring
It is given as a rapid IV push for fastest effect
It replaces the need for systemic steroids
pa-peds-geri-l04.why: IV magnesium (25 to 50 mg/kg) is a bronchodilator adjunct for severe exacerbations but can cause hypotension, so it is infused slowly with monitoring rather than pushed. It does not replace steroids and is used in children when indicated, not withheld outright.

pa-peds-geri-l05.q: Why does ondansetron reduce the need for IV fluids in pediatric gastroenteritis?
choices: It directly rehydrates the child
It reduces vomiting enough that oral rehydration solution is tolerated and succeeds
It treats the underlying viral infection
It increases gastric emptying to speed digestion
pa-peds-geri-l05.why: By controlling vomiting, ondansetron lets a child keep down oral rehydration solution, avoiding an IV start; it does not rehydrate, treat the virus, or act as a prokinetic itself.

pa-peds-geri-l05.q: A newborn with bilious vomiting needs which evaluation first, and why is time-sensitivity so high?
choices: Outpatient ultrasound within a week, since bilious vomiting is usually benign reflux
Emergent upper GI series or surgical consultation, because midgut volvulus can infarct the bowel within hours
A stool culture, since bacterial gastroenteritis is the most likely cause
Reassurance and observation for 24 hours before any imaging
pa-peds-geri-l05.why: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise, and delayed diagnosis risks bowel infarction within hours, so emergent imaging or surgical evaluation is required. Reflux is never bilious, and observation risks catastrophic bowel loss.

pa-peds-geri-l06.q: Why does timing of IVIG matter in Kawasaki disease?
choices: IVIG only works if given after day 10 of fever
IVIG given within 10 days of fever onset substantially lowers the risk of coronary artery aneurysm
Timing has no effect on outcomes
IVIG must be given within the first 24 hours or it is ineffective
pa-peds-geri-l06.why: Treatment within the first 10 days of illness reduces aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to about 4 percent; waiting past day 10 or believing timing does not matter both increase risk. A strict 24-hour window is not the actual cutoff.

pa-peds-geri-l06.q: What differentiates preseptal from orbital cellulitis on exam?
choices: Preseptal cellulitis causes pain with eye movement and proptosis
Orbital cellulitis causes pain with eye movement, proptosis, or restricted extraocular motion, while preseptal does not
Both are managed identically with oral antibiotics
Fever distinguishes the two conditions reliably
pa-peds-geri-l06.why: Orbital (postseptal) involvement affects the muscles and contents behind the septum, producing pain with movement, proptosis, and restricted motion, while preseptal cellulitis spares these. Fever can occur with either, and management differs (oral vs IV antibiotics and imaging).

pa-peds-geri-l07.q: Why can an older adult's creatinine look normal despite significantly reduced kidney function?
choices: Aging kidneys produce less creatinine naturally
Reduced muscle mass lowers creatinine production, masking a falling GFR
Dehydration always lowers creatinine in older adults
Creatinine is not affected by muscle mass at any age
pa-peds-geri-l07.why: Creatinine is a byproduct of muscle metabolism; with age-related muscle loss, less is produced, so a 'normal' creatinine can hide a substantially reduced GFR. Dehydration would raise, not lower, creatinine, and muscle mass does affect creatinine at every age.

pa-peds-geri-l07.q: What is the practical implication of a lower fever threshold in older adults?
choices: Older adults should be considered afebrile unless temperature exceeds 39 C
A temperature increase as small as 1.1 C above baseline, or a single reading above 37.8 C, should be treated as a possible fever
Fever thresholds are identical to those used in children
Temperature is not a useful vital sign in geriatric patients
pa-peds-geri-l07.why: Because baseline temperature and febrile response both drop with age, smaller elevations count as fever in older adults, and roughly 20 to 30 percent of serious infections are afebrile altogether, so a modest rise deserves attention. Waiting for 39 C or discounting temperature risks missing serious infection.

pa-peds-geri-l08.q: Why is a geriatric syndrome described as arising from several small failures rather than one clear cause?
choices: Because a single organ failure always explains the presentation
Because reduced reserve across multiple systems (vision, gait, cognition, medications) combines to produce one visible problem like a fall
Because geriatric syndromes are psychiatric in origin
Because they only occur in patients with a single chronic disease
pa-peds-geri-l08.why: Falls, delirium, and similar syndromes typically result from the additive effect of several modest deficits across systems, not one isolated cause, which is why a full multifactorial workup is needed rather than searching for a single diagnosis.

pa-peds-geri-l08.q: Why does a hip fracture carry such high one-year mortality in older adults?
choices: The fracture itself is directly fatal in most cases
It triggers a cascade of immobility, deconditioning, delirium, and complications like pneumonia or clots that compound baseline frailty
It is unrelated to overall mortality risk
It only affects mortality if surgery is delayed more than a month
pa-peds-geri-l08.why: The fracture is rarely fatal on its own; the 20 to 30 percent one-year mortality comes from downstream immobility, deconditioning, delirium, and complications layered onto already reduced reserve. Surgical delay matters but is not the sole driver of the statistic.

pa-peds-geri-l09.q: What is a prescribing cascade, and why is it dangerous?
choices: A pharmacy error that delivers the wrong drug
A new medication is prescribed to treat a side effect of an existing medication, misread as a new disease
A patient taking fewer than 5 medications
A planned taper of a benzodiazepine
pa-peds-geri-l09.why: A prescribing cascade happens when a drug's side effect is mistaken for a new illness and treated with another drug, compounding risk instead of removing the cause. It is not a dispensing error, and taking under 5 medications is the opposite of polypharmacy.

pa-peds-geri-l09.q: Why are NSAIDs high-risk in older adults even without a diagnosed kidney problem?
choices: They have no meaningful risk in this population
They can reduce renal blood flow and precipitate acute kidney injury, especially combined with an ACE inhibitor or diuretic
They only cause gastrointestinal bleeding, never renal effects
They are metabolized identically regardless of age
pa-peds-geri-l09.why: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole and reduce renal perfusion, which is usually tolerated but becomes dangerous when combined with an ACE inhibitor/ARB and a diuretic (the triple whammy), risking acute kidney injury. GI bleeding is a separate, additional risk, not the only one.

pa-peds-geri-l10.q: What is the key difference between an advance directive and a POLST in New Jersey?
choices: They are legally identical documents with different names
An advance directive states general wishes or names a proxy, while a POLST is a signed medical order acted on directly in an emergency
A POLST only applies in hospice settings
An advance directive overrides a POLST whenever both exist
pa-peds-geri-l10.why: An advance directive expresses wishes and may appoint a proxy but is not itself an order; a POLST is a signed, portable medical order that clinicians follow directly. POLST is not hospice-exclusive, and in practice the POLST, being an actionable order, guides immediate care.

pa-peds-geri-l10.q: Why is palliative care distinct from hospice?
choices: Palliative care requires a prognosis of 6 months or less, identical to hospice
Palliative care can be provided at any stage of illness alongside curative treatment, while hospice requires forgoing curative treatment with a prognosis of 6 months or less
Palliative care is only for cancer patients
Hospice and palliative care are the same program under different names
pa-peds-geri-l10.why: Palliative care focuses on symptom relief and can run alongside curative treatment at any stage of disease, whereas hospice specifically requires a 6-month-or-less prognosis and forgoing curative intent. It is not disease-specific and the two are distinct programs.

quiz.q: A 30-month-old speaks in two- to three-word phrases that are about half intelligible to a stranger and plays alongside other children without interacting. What is the correct assessment?
choices: Normal development for age; a 3-year-old is expected to reach 75 percent intelligibility and parallel play is typical before that
Delayed language and social development requiring urgent referral
Autism spectrum disorder confirmed by this presentation alone
Hearing loss confirmed, requiring immediate cochlear implant referral
quiz.why: At 30 months, phrase speech with partial intelligibility and parallel play are both within the normal range on the way to the 3-year anchors. A single snapshot cannot diagnose autism or confirm hearing loss, and there is no missed deadline here to justify urgent referral.

quiz.q: A previously toilet-trained 4-year-old begins wetting the bed and refusing to speak in school after his parents' separation. Exam and urinalysis are normal. What is the best next step?
choices: Order renal ultrasound to rule out structural urinary disease
Reassure that regression under stress is common, but screen for other stressors and consider behavioral referral if it persists
Diagnose a urinary tract infection empirically
Assume abuse and report immediately without further history
quiz.why: Regression of an acquired skill during major stress like divorce is common and usually resolves with support, but persistent regression warrants screening. A normal exam and urinalysis argue against structural or infectious causes, and regression alone is not sufficient grounds to report abuse without other red flags.

quiz.q: During a confidential HEEADSSS interview, a 15-year-old discloses that she has a detailed plan and means to end her life this week. How does the confidentiality rule apply?
choices: Confidentiality is absolute and this cannot be disclosed to anyone
Only law enforcement can be told, not parents
This is one of the stated limits to confidentiality; her safety must be addressed immediately, including involving a parent or guardian
The interview must be redone with a parent present before any action is taken
quiz.why: Risk of harm to the patient is a standard, explicitly stated limit to adolescent confidentiality, so immediate safety action, including parental involvement, is required. Confidentiality is never absolute when safety is at risk, and delaying to redo the interview would waste critical time.

quiz.q: A 7-month-old girl is brought in for a well visit. She sits without support and transfers objects hand to hand but is not yet crawling. Which statement is correct?
choices: Crawling is expected by 7 months and its absence is a red flag
She should already be walking independently
This pattern suggests global developmental delay requiring immediate MRI
This is within the normal range; crawling and pulling to stand are 9-month anchors, not 7-month ones
quiz.why: Sitting without support and hand-to-hand transfer are expected by about 6 to 8 months, and crawling is expected around 9 months, so its absence at 7 months is not yet a red flag. Walking is a 12-month milestone, and one age-appropriate finding does not justify imaging.

quiz.q: A 1-day-old term newborn is visibly jaundiced on the face and chest. What is the significance of jaundice appearing in the first 24 hours of life?
choices: It is always pathologic and requires prompt bilirubin measurement and evaluation
It is always physiologic and resolves without workup
It only matters if the baby is premature
It indicates breastfeeding failure exclusively
quiz.why: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is never physiologic; physiologic jaundice appears after the first 24 hours and peaks around day 3 to 5. This finding demands prompt bilirubin testing regardless of gestational age, and breastfeeding jaundice would not present this early.

quiz.q: Paramedics call in a report on a 3-year-old found by EMS: crying loudly, clinging to the parent, and pulling away from the stethoscope. What does this appearance suggest on the pediatric assessment triangle?
choices: Abnormal appearance suggesting critical illness
A reassuring appearance; vigorous resistance and consolability by a caregiver are normal, healthy responses
Impending respiratory failure
Circulatory shock requiring immediate IV access
quiz.why: A child who fights exam and is consolable by a caregiver shows normal tone, interactiveness, and consolability, the reassuring pattern on the triangle. It is the quiet, unresisting child who is more concerning, not this one, and nothing here points to respiratory or circulatory failure.

quiz.q: A 7-year-old weighs 24 kg by scale. Using the age-based estimate (age x 2) + 8, how does this compare, and what should you do?
choices: The estimate must be used even though an actual weight exists
The discrepancy means the scale is broken and should be recalibrated before use
The estimate would predict 22 kg; use the actual scale weight of 24 kg for dosing since it is available
Round up to the nearest length-tape color regardless of the scale weight
quiz.why: The formula gives an estimate for when a scale is unavailable; once an actual weight is obtained, it should be used for dosing since it is more accurate. A 2 kg difference does not indicate a broken scale, and there is no reason to default to an estimate when real data exists.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old in septic shock has a systolic blood pressure of 78 mmHg. Using the formula 70 + (2 x age), how should this be interpreted?
choices: Normal, since 78 is above the newborn threshold
Hypotensive only if the heart rate is also elevated
Not interpretable without a diastolic pressure
Hypotensive, since the age-based threshold for a 5-year-old is 80 mmHg
quiz.why: 70 + (2 x 5) = 80, so a systolic of 78 falls below threshold and counts as hypotension, a late and ominous sign in a child already presumed septic. This determination does not require a concurrent heart rate or diastolic value to apply the formula.

quiz.q: A 1-month-old girl has a rectal temperature of 38.1 C. Regardless of how well she appears, what is the required approach?
choices: Full workup including blood, urine, and CSF cultures, empiric antibiotics, and admission, because she is under 28 days
Risk-stratify with inflammatory markers and consider outpatient management if low risk
Send home with close follow-up if she is feeding well
Treat as viral illness without further testing
quiz.why: Under 28 days, fever mandates the full evaluation and empiric treatment regardless of appearance, since clinical appearance is unreliable at this age for excluding serious bacterial infection. Risk-stratified outpatient management and simple reassurance both apply to older infants (29 to 60 days and beyond), not neonates.

quiz.q: A febrile 50-day-old has a procalcitonin of 0.8 ng/mL. What does this single elevated marker most likely change about management?
choices: Nothing; procalcitonin is not used in this age group
It shifts the infant out of the low-risk category, favoring further workup such as CSF studies and likely admission
It confirms viral illness and rules out bacterial infection
It mandates immediate surgery
quiz.why: A procalcitonin above about 0.5 ng/mL is one of the risk-stratification markers in the 29-to-60-day group; an elevated value moves the infant toward the higher-risk pathway requiring more workup. It does not confirm a viral cause, and procalcitonin is in fact a standard tool at this age, not irrelevant.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old with no history of febrile seizures has a first simple febrile seizure witnessed by both parents, lasting 4 minutes, with full return to baseline. What imaging or lab workup is indicated for the seizure itself?
choices: EEG only
CT head emergently
None specifically for the seizure; workup should target the fever source
Lumbar puncture regardless of exam findings
quiz.why: A simple febrile seizure in a well-appearing, fully immunized child needs no LP, imaging, or EEG; effort should go toward identifying the fever source instead. None of the listed tests are indicated by the seizure itself when criteria for simple febrile seizure are met.

quiz.q: A 6-week-old with bronchiolitis has intermittent pauses in breathing lasting several seconds witnessed by the parent. Why does this change management compared with an older infant with the same wheezing?
choices: It does not change management; apnea is expected and benign in bronchiolitis at any age
It indicates the infant needs bronchodilators
It confirms a bacterial superinfection requiring antibiotics
Infants under about 2 months are at higher risk for apnea with bronchiolitis, which usually prompts admission for monitoring
quiz.why: Young infants, particularly under 2 months, are at increased risk for apnea with bronchiolitis (especially RSV), which is a recognized indication for admission and monitoring rather than outpatient management. Bronchodilators and antibiotics are not indicated by apnea, and apnea is never treated as benign at this age.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old with croup and stridor at rest is treated with nebulized epinephrine and improves markedly within 15 minutes. The parent asks to go home right away. What is correct?
choices: Observe for 2 to 4 hours for rebound stridor as the epinephrine effect wears off, then reassess before discharge
Discharge immediately since symptoms resolved
Admit automatically regardless of response
Repeat epinephrine immediately regardless of current status
quiz.why: Nebulized epinephrine's effect is short-lived, and stridor can rebound as it wears off, so observation for 2 to 4 hours is required before safe discharge. Immediate discharge risks missing rebound, admission is not automatic if the extended observation goes well, and repeat dosing is not given without renewed symptoms.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old with known asthma has a respiratory rate of 40, uses accessory muscles, but has clear, easily audible wheezing throughout both lung fields. Compared to a child with a silent chest, what does this tell you?
choices: Audible wheezing throughout the lungs is worse than a silent chest
Audible wheezing indicates air is still moving, which is a better sign than a silent chest where minimal air movement produces no sound
Wheezing quality has no relationship to severity
A silent chest means the exacerbation has resolved
quiz.why: Wheezing requires airflow to generate sound, so audible wheeze, while still concerning, reflects more air movement than a silent chest, where minimal airflow produces no breath sounds at all and signals impending failure. A silent chest is a deterioration, not resolution.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old has 5 days of fever, cough, and tachypnea with a respiratory rate of 42. The chest radiograph shows a focal right lower lobe infiltrate. What is the first-line outpatient treatment?
choices: Azithromycin alone
Ceftriaxone IM as a single dose only
Amoxicillin at about 90 mg/kg/day
No antibiotics, since pneumonia in children is almost always viral
quiz.why: High-dose amoxicillin (about 90 mg/kg/day) is first-line for typical bacterial community-acquired pneumonia in children. Azithromycin is reserved for atypical coverage, IM ceftriaxone is not the standard first-line outpatient choice, and a focal infiltrate with this clinical picture is treated, not observed as presumed viral.

quiz.q: A 15-month-old with mild dehydration from gastroenteritis is tolerating oral rehydration solution well at home. What total volume should the caregiver aim for, and over what timeframe?
choices: 100 mL/kg over 4 hours
Unlimited water as tolerated
20 mL/kg as a single rapid bolus
50 mL/kg over 4 hours, given a small amount frequently
quiz.why: Mild dehydration (3 to 5 percent) targets 50 mL/kg of oral rehydration solution over 4 hours, given in small frequent amounts to improve tolerance. 100 mL/kg is the moderate-dehydration target, plain water lacks electrolytes, and a rapid IV-style bolus is not how oral rehydration is given.

quiz.q: An infant with severe dehydration (about 12 percent) is lethargic with a prolonged capillary refill and a weak pulse. What is the correct initial fluid step?
choices: A 20 mL/kg isotonic IV bolus, repeated as needed based on reassessment
Oral rehydration solution 100 mL/kg over 4 hours
Ondansetron alone followed by observation
Maintenance IV fluids without a bolus
quiz.why: Severe dehydration with signs of poor perfusion requires an isotonic IV bolus (20 mL/kg), reassessed and repeated as needed, not oral rehydration, which this child cannot safely tolerate. Maintenance-rate fluids alone would not correct the deficit quickly enough, and antiemetics alone do not address volume loss.

quiz.q: A 4-week-old boy has increasingly frequent nonbilious vomiting after most feeds and a palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium. What is the diagnosis and appropriate imaging?
choices: Malrotation with volvulus; emergent upper GI series
Pyloric stenosis; abdominal ultrasound
Intussusception; abdominal ultrasound looking for a target sign
Necrotizing enterocolitis; abdominal radiograph
quiz.why: A palpable olive mass with progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting around 3 to 6 weeks of age is classic for pyloric stenosis, confirmed with ultrasound showing a thickened, elongated pylorus. Volvulus produces bilious vomiting, intussusception presents differently (often with lethargy and colicky pain), and NEC occurs in a different clinical context, usually premature infants.

quiz.q: A 7-year-old presents with a fever of 40.1 C for 2 days, a diffuse petechial rash that does not blanch, and neck stiffness. What is the priority order of action?
choices: Wait for lumbar puncture results before starting antibiotics
Start oral antibiotics and discharge with follow-up
Obtain blood cultures and give empiric antibiotics immediately, then pursue lumbar puncture as feasible
Observe for 4 hours to see if the rash blanches over time
quiz.why: Fever with non-blanching rash and meningismus raises strong concern for meningococcemia, where delay in antibiotics increases mortality; cultures and empiric IV antibiotics should not wait for LP results. Oral antibiotics and outpatient management are inadequate, and observation risks rapid deterioration in a condition that can progress to shock within hours.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old meets criteria for Kawasaki disease on day 6 of fever. Which combination is correct initial treatment, and what does it aim to prevent?
choices: Oral antibiotics only, aiming to treat presumed streptococcal infection
IVIG alone without aspirin, aiming to reduce fever only
High-dose steroids alone, aiming to prevent rash progression
IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, aiming to reduce the risk of coronary artery aneurysm
quiz.why: IVIG with aspirin is standard treatment for Kawasaki disease and is specifically aimed at reducing coronary artery aneurysm risk, the disease's most feared complication. Antibiotics do not treat this vasculitis, IVIG is paired with aspirin (not given alone), and steroids are not first-line, so none of the other options address the aneurysm risk correctly.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old fell off a bike, struck the back of his head, vomited once, but has a GCS of 15, no palpable skull fracture, and no other findings. According to PECARN, what is appropriate?
choices: Observation, since isolated vomiting without other high-risk PECARN predictors supports a period of observation rather than immediate imaging
CT head immediately given any vomiting
Discharge with no observation or instructions
Skull radiograph instead of CT
quiz.why: PECARN treats isolated vomiting without other predictors (altered mental status, palpable skull fracture, severe headache, LOC, etc.) as intermediate risk, supporting observation over immediate CT to avoid unnecessary radiation. Discharge with no follow-up ignores the vomiting entirely, and skull radiographs are not part of the PECARN pathway.

quiz.q: A teacher tells a PA she saw a 7-year-old's father strike him and wants to know if she has a legal duty to report in New Jersey. What should the PA explain?
choices: Only physicians and teachers are mandated reporters in New Jersey
New Jersey requires any person with reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused to report to 1-877-NJ-ABUSE, and good-faith reporting carries legal immunity
She should confirm with the family before reporting
Reporting is optional if the child denies the abuse
quiz.why: New Jersey's mandated reporting law applies to any person, not a restricted list of professions, and good-faith reports are protected from liability. Confirming with the family first could endanger the child and undermine the investigation, and a child's denial does not remove the duty to report reasonable suspicion.

quiz.q: An 85-year-old with baseline mild kidney disease is prescribed a new medication dosed by weight and renal function. Why is estimating GFR before dosing especially important in this population?
choices: Because older adults metabolize drugs faster than younger adults
Because GFR estimation is only relevant in dialysis patients
Because a normal-appearing creatinine can mask significantly reduced GFR from lower muscle mass, risking drug toxicity if dosed as if renal function were normal
Because weight-based dosing is never used in geriatric patients
quiz.why: Reduced muscle mass lowers creatinine production independent of true kidney function, so relying on creatinine alone risks underestimating impairment and overdosing renally cleared medications. Older adults generally metabolize and clear drugs more slowly, not faster, and GFR estimation is relevant well before dialysis-level disease.

quiz.q: A 77-year-old presents with new shortness of breath and generalized weakness but denies chest pain. ECG shows ST depression in the inferior leads. What should this presentation prompt?
choices: Ruling out cardiac causes since chest pain is absent
Reassurance that ECG changes without pain are usually benign
Immediate discharge with outpatient cardiology follow-up
Continued workup for myocardial infarction, since painless presentations are common in older adults
quiz.why: About a third of MIs in older adults are painless, presenting instead as dyspnea, weakness, syncope, or confusion, so absence of chest pain should not stop the workup, especially with ischemic ECG changes. ECG changes are never dismissed as benign, and this presentation warrants continued inpatient evaluation, not discharge.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old falls from standing, strikes his head, has no loss of consciousness, and is not on any blood thinner. His GCS is 15 and exam is normal. How does age alone factor into his workup compared to a 40-year-old with the identical presentation?
choices: Age over 65 is itself a risk factor that lowers the threshold for CT imaging even without anticoagulation
Age changes nothing about head injury decision-making
CT is only indicated if he is on anticoagulation
Age only matters for musculoskeletal injuries, not head injuries
quiz.why: Age 65 and older is an independent risk factor in adult head injury decision rules, lowering the threshold for CT even without anticoagulation or loss of consciousness, unlike in younger, low-risk patients. Anticoagulation is a separate additional trigger, not the only reason age matters here.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old presents after a mechanical fall and denies any warning symptoms, but the family reports she seemed to briefly lose consciousness beforehand. Why does distinguishing mechanical fall from syncope matter?
choices: It does not change management once the injury is treated
A syncopal cause requires cardiac and neurologic workup (such as ECG and orthostatics) beyond simply treating the fall injury
Only mechanical falls require follow-up
Syncope in older adults is always benign and needs no further testing
quiz.why: If the fall was actually syncope, an underlying cardiac arrhythmia or other serious cause may be present and needs evaluation (ECG, orthostatics, medication review) beyond just treating the resulting injury. Treating it as purely mechanical could miss a dangerous, recurrent cause, and syncope in this age group is not assumed benign.

quiz.q: A 90-year-old with dementia has been at her baseline cognitive level, conversant and consistent, for the past several days according to her caregiver, though her memory is poor overall. What does this argue against?
choices: Dementia, since a stable pattern rules it out
Nothing; this pattern is diagnostic of delirium
Delirium, since delirium requires an acute, fluctuating change from baseline, which is absent here
Any cognitive disorder, since memory loss alone is not a diagnosis
quiz.why: Delirium is defined by an acute, fluctuating change in attention from a person's baseline; a stable, unchanged cognitive pattern over days argues against a superimposed delirium. It is consistent with chronic dementia, not evidence against it, and does not by itself exclude a cognitive disorder diagnosis in general.

quiz.q: A nursing home resident is found with a stage 3 pressure injury on the sacrum during a visit for an unrelated complaint. What is required regardless of the chief complaint?
choices: No action, since it is unrelated to today's visit
Immediate discharge back to the facility without comment
Treating it only if the patient specifically requests it
Careful documentation of the finding on arrival, since pressure injuries are a marker of care quality and potential neglect
quiz.why: Pressure injuries must be documented on arrival because they can reflect neglect or inadequate care and have legal and clinical significance regardless of the presenting complaint. Ignoring or deferring documentation until requested would miss a required safety and quality marker.

quiz.q: An 84-year-old on chronic opioids for back pain is started on a benzodiazepine for anxiety by a different prescriber who is unaware of the opioid use. What is the primary concern with this combination?
choices: Additive CNS and respiratory depression, increasing fall and overdose risk, a key reason benzodiazepines are high-risk under Beers criteria
No meaningful interaction exists between these drug classes
The combination only affects blood pressure
Benzodiazepines counteract opioid sedation, making the combination protective
quiz.why: Benzodiazepines and opioids both cause CNS and respiratory depression, and combining them multiplies sedation, fall, and overdose risk, which is exactly why benzodiazepines are flagged in the Beers criteria for older adults. They do not counteract each other, and the concern is not primarily about blood pressure.

quiz.q: A family asks why their mother with moderate dementia was recently started on an antipsychotic for agitation, and why the PA is now recommending it be stopped. What is the correct explanation?
choices: Antipsychotics are first-line and should be continued indefinitely for dementia-related agitation
Antipsychotics in dementia carry a Beers-flagged increased risk of stroke and death and should be reserved for situations where non-drug measures have failed and risks are addressed
Antipsychotics have no significant risks in older adults with dementia
The medication should be stopped only if the family requests it
quiz.why: Antipsychotics used for behavioral symptoms of dementia carry an increased risk of stroke and mortality, which is why the Beers criteria flag them and why non-pharmacologic approaches are preferred first. They are not risk-free, not indefinite first-line therapy, and the decision to stop should be driven by clinical risk, not solely by family preference.

quiz.q: An 83-year-old with type 2 diabetes on glyburide has recurrent episodes of confusion and sweating in the late afternoon. What is the most likely explanation and why is this drug particularly risky in this population?
choices: Glyburide causes hyperglycemia, unrelated to her symptoms
Her symptoms are unrelated to medication and reflect normal aging
Glyburide is a long-acting sulfonylurea with a high risk of prolonged hypoglycemia in older adults, especially with reduced renal clearance
Glyburide has no meaningful hypoglycemia risk compared to other diabetes medications
quiz.why: Glyburide is a long-acting sulfonylurea that older adults, especially those with reduced renal clearance, metabolize more slowly, leading to prolonged and sometimes severe hypoglycemia, which is why it is specifically flagged in the Beers criteria. The symptoms described (confusion, sweating) are classic hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia or unrelated aging changes.

quiz.q: A 79-year-old with mild cognitive impairment wants to appoint someone to make medical decisions if she becomes unable to in the future, but is not ready to specify treatment preferences in detail. Which tool is most appropriate now?
choices: A POLST, since it applies to anyone regardless of current health status
Hospice enrollment, to formalize her wishes
Nothing can be done until she loses capacity
A proxy directive naming a healthcare agent, part of a New Jersey advance directive
quiz.why: A proxy directive lets her name a decision-maker without committing to detailed treatment instructions now, which fits her stated preference; this is a standard component of a New Jersey advance directive. A POLST is meant for patients with serious illness needing actionable current orders, hospice requires a terminal prognosis, and she can act now while she still has capacity.

quiz.q: An 88-year-old with advanced dementia is unable to answer questions about her medical history, name a proxy, or express understanding of her situation. Who determines whether she has decision-making capacity for a proposed treatment?
choices: The treating clinician, assessing her ability to communicate a choice, understand, appreciate, and reason about the specific decision at hand
A judge only, since capacity is strictly a legal determination
Her family, regardless of her own responses
Capacity does not need to be assessed if she has a dementia diagnosis
quiz.why: Capacity is a clinical, decision-specific determination made by the treating clinician using the four components (choice, understanding, appreciation, reasoning), distinct from the legal concept of competency determined by a court. A dementia diagnosis alone does not establish incapacity, and family preference does not substitute for the patient's own assessed capacity.

quiz.q: A home health aide reports that an elderly client's daughter, who controls her finances, recently stopped buying her prescribed medications and the client has lost significant weight. What category of concern does this represent, and what is the initial step?
choices: Normal caregiver stress, requiring no action
Possible financial exploitation and neglect; interview the patient alone and report to the appropriate New Jersey adult protective services agency
A dietary preference issue only
Action is not warranted unless the client explicitly requests help
quiz.why: Withholding needed medications and resulting weight loss under a caregiver's financial control are signs of neglect and possible financial exploitation, which affect roughly 1 in 10 community-dwelling older adults; the key first step is a private interview followed by reporting. Waiting for the client to ask for help ignores that fear or dependence on the abuser often prevents disclosure.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old boy is not yet using sentences and mostly grunts and points to communicate; his parents say he has never said a clear word. What is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Reassure that boys often talk later than girls and recheck in a year
Diagnose autism spectrum disorder based on speech alone
Refer for hearing evaluation and speech-language assessment, since this is well past expected anchors for word and sentence use
No action needed since he can point to indicate needs
quiz.why: By 4 years, children are expected to speak in sentences; a complete absence of words is far outside normal variation and warrants hearing and speech evaluation regardless of sex. Nonverbal communication like pointing does not substitute for expected language milestones, and speech delay alone is not sufficient to diagnose autism.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old with fever and tachycardia has cool extremities, a capillary refill of 3 seconds, and a blood pressure of 100/60, which is normal for age. Why should this still concern you?
choices: Normal blood pressure rules out any degree of shock
Cool extremities in a febrile child are always due to ambient temperature
No further evaluation is needed if blood pressure is normal
Compensated shock can exist with a normal blood pressure; perfusion findings like cool extremities and delayed refill matter more at this stage
quiz.why: Children maintain blood pressure through compensation until late in shock, so cool extremities and delayed capillary refill can signal compensated shock despite a normal-for-age blood pressure. Attributing cool extremities to room temperature alone would miss a child who needs active resuscitation.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old is quiet, staring blankly, and not interacting with the parent despite normal work of breathing and warm, pink skin. What does the pediatric assessment triangle suggest about the urgency here?
choices: This is concerning; abnormal appearance alone, even with normal breathing and circulation, warrants urgent evaluation for causes like hypoglycemia, toxin, or CNS process
This is reassuring since breathing and circulation are normal
This pattern always indicates a primary respiratory problem
This pattern indicates dehydration specifically
quiz.why: Appearance reflects brain perfusion and function; an abnormal appearance by itself, even when breathing and circulation look normal on the triangle, is urgent and prompts evaluation for hypoglycemia, toxic ingestion, seizure, or infection. It does not specifically indicate a respiratory or dehydration cause without other supporting findings.

quiz.q: A 35-day-old infant with fever undergoes risk stratification. Urinalysis is negative, procalcitonin is 0.3 ng/mL, CRP is 12 mg/L, and ANC is 3,800. What does this profile support?
choices: Automatic lumbar puncture and admission regardless of these results
Low-risk classification, potentially supporting close outpatient follow-up without LP per current risk-stratification guidance
Immediate discharge with no follow-up plan
A diagnosis of urinary tract infection based on these labs
quiz.why: All markers fall below the risk-stratification thresholds (procalcitonin under 0.5, CRP under 20, ANC under about 4,000 to 5,200) and a negative urinalysis, supporting a low-risk designation that can allow outpatient management with close follow-up rather than mandatory LP and admission. The urinalysis is explicitly negative, so it does not support a UTI diagnosis, and discharge without any follow-up plan is not appropriate even when low-risk.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old has a fever of 38.9 C, is fussy but consolable, drinking fluids, and has no localizing findings on exam. What is the most appropriate approach?
choices: Full sepsis workup including lumbar puncture regardless of exam
Empiric antibiotics without any evaluation
Targeted history and exam for a source, since appearance and exam are much more reliable at this age than in early infancy
Admission for observation regardless of findings
quiz.why: By 3 years, clinical appearance and physical exam are reliable enough to guide a focused evaluation for a fever source, unlike the unreliable exam in very young infants that mandates full workups. Empiric antibiotics without evaluation and automatic admission are not warranted in a well-appearing, consolable, hydrated child with a normal exam.

quiz.q: A previously healthy 3-year-old has a first febrile seizure at 39.5 C, generalized, lasting 2 minutes, with full recovery within 10 minutes. The parents ask if this means their child has epilepsy. What should they be told?
choices: Yes, this is epilepsy and requires lifelong antiseizure medication
Only if the seizure recurs within 24 hours does it count as epilepsy
The diagnosis cannot be determined without an EEG
No; a simple febrile seizure is not epilepsy, though there is a modestly increased recurrence risk with future fevers, and no daily medication is needed
quiz.why: Simple febrile seizures are a benign, age-limited phenomenon distinct from epilepsy, and children have a modestly increased risk of another febrile seizure but do not need daily antiseizure medication or routine EEG. Recurrence within 24 hours would make this complex rather than diagnostic of epilepsy, and EEG is not required to make this distinction.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old with a first-time wheezing episode and a low-grade fever is found to have a normal chest radiograph and improves substantially with albuterol. What does the response to albuterol suggest about the underlying process compared to bronchiolitis?
choices: It suggests reactive airway disease or early asthma, since bronchiolitis in an infant typically does not respond meaningfully to bronchodilators
It confirms bronchiolitis, since bronchiolitis always improves with albuterol
The response to albuterol has no diagnostic significance at this age
It confirms pneumonia
quiz.why: Bronchiolitis is caused by inflammation and mucus in small airways in infants and shows little consistent bronchodilator response, whereas a 4-year-old with true bronchospasm improving on albuterol points toward reactive airway disease or asthma rather than typical bronchiolitis, which is also mostly a disease of infants under 2. A normal chest film argues against pneumonia here.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old has a barky cough but no stridor at rest and only mild stridor with crying or agitation. What severity of croup does this represent, and what treatment is indicated?
choices: Severe croup requiring nebulized epinephrine and prolonged observation
Mild-to-moderate croup; dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg is still indicated even without stridor at rest
No treatment needed since there is no stridor at rest
Antibiotics, since this pattern suggests bacterial tracheitis
quiz.why: Dexamethasone at 0.6 mg/kg is recommended across croup severities, including mild-to-moderate disease without stridor at rest, because it reduces progression and return visits. Nebulized epinephrine is reserved for stridor at rest, withholding all treatment ignores dexamethasone's benefit even in milder disease, and this presentation does not suggest a bacterial process needing antibiotics.

quiz.q: A 3-month-old has 2 weeks of paroxysmal coughing fits followed by apnea and cyanosis, without a classic whoop. Why might this diagnosis be missed if the provider is only listening for the whoop?
choices: Because the whoop is present in essentially all cases and easy to hear
Because pertussis does not occur in infants under 6 months
Because young infants often present atypically with apnea and cyanosis rather than the classic whoop, which is more common in older children
Because apnea and cyanosis rule out pertussis entirely
quiz.why: Infants, especially young ones, often lack the classic inspiratory whoop and instead present with apneic, cyanotic episodes, making the diagnosis easy to miss if a provider is anchored on the whoop as a required finding. Pertussis absolutely occurs in this age group and is in fact more dangerous here, and apnea/cyanosis are consistent with, not exclusionary for, pertussis.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old with moderate dehydration is prescribed oral rehydration solution but keeps refusing to drink from a cup. What technique is recommended to improve success?
choices: Switch immediately to IV fluids without trying an alternative oral method
Allow unlimited free drinking of any preferred beverage
Wait several hours and reattempt the same method
Give small volumes, such as 5 mL, by syringe every 1 to 2 minutes
quiz.why: Giving oral rehydration solution in small syringe volumes every 1 to 2 minutes is the recommended technique to improve tolerance and success when cup drinking fails, before escalating to IV fluids. Free drinking of any beverage risks inadequate electrolyte content, and simply repeating a failed method without changing technique wastes time.

quiz.q: A 9-month-old has episodes of drawing his knees to his chest and crying, alternating with periods of appearing well, and passes a stool with blood and mucus resembling currant jelly. What does the stool finding add to the clinical picture?
choices: It reinforces the diagnosis of intussusception, supporting urgent ultrasound and likely therapeutic enema
It is a nonspecific finding unrelated to the intermittent symptoms
It suggests bacterial gastroenteritis as the primary diagnosis
It confirms pyloric stenosis
quiz.why: Currant jelly stool, from mucosal ischemia and sloughing at the intussuscepted segment, is a classic (though late) finding that reinforces the intermittent-lethargy pattern already concerning for intussusception, prompting urgent ultrasound and likely enema reduction. It does not fit pyloric stenosis, which does not cause bloody stool, and simple gastroenteritis does not typically produce this specific combination.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old has widespread urticarial wheals that blanch completely with pressure, no fever, and a known new food exposure. How does the blanching finding guide your evaluation?
choices: Blanching lesions are treated identically to non-blanching purpura and require blood cultures
Blanching argues against a vasculitic or hematologic process like meningococcemia, supporting an allergic etiology instead
Blanching is not a useful distinguishing feature in pediatric rashes
Blanching indicates the rash is caused by a viral exanthem specifically
quiz.why: Blanching under pressure indicates the color comes from dilated vessels rather than extravasated blood, arguing against the non-blanching purpura pattern of meningococcemia or vasculitis and fitting better with an allergic or urticarial process, especially with a clear trigger and no fever. It does not specifically diagnose a viral exanthem, and blanching lesions do not warrant the same emergent workup as non-blanching purpura with fever.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old meets 3 of the 5 classic clinical criteria for Kawasaki disease with fever for 7 days, plus has echocardiography showing coronary artery changes. How should incomplete criteria be handled here?
choices: Kawasaki disease is excluded because fewer than 4 criteria are present
Treatment should be withheld until all 5 criteria are eventually met
Incomplete Kawasaki disease can still be diagnosed and treated, particularly when supportive findings like coronary changes on echocardiogram are present
This presentation should be reclassified as scarlet fever automatically
quiz.why: Incomplete (atypical) Kawasaki disease is a recognized entity when fewer than 4 criteria are met but supporting laboratory or echocardiographic findings (like coronary abnormalities) are present, and it still warrants treatment to prevent progression. Waiting for all criteria to appear risks delaying IVIG past the window that best protects the coronary arteries, and nothing here specifically points to scarlet fever.

quiz.q: A 15-month-old is found by his mother in an empty adult bedroom, unresponsive with a bruise on his forehead consistent with a fall from a changing table she describes. Developmentally, what should you check to help evaluate this account?
choices: His vaccination record only
His growth curve only
Nothing further; the explanation should be accepted as given
Whether he has reached milestones consistent with the ability to roll, pull to stand, or otherwise access the height described
quiz.why: Matching the child's actual developmental abilities (rolling, pulling to stand, climbing) against the mechanism described is a core part of evaluating a concerning injury story, since an implausible mechanism relative to developmental stage is a red flag for abuse. Vaccination and growth records do not address whether the story is physically plausible, and accepting any explanation uncritically undermines the required safety evaluation.

quiz.q: A 71-year-old with well-controlled hypertension takes no other medications and has a stable, slightly elevated baseline temperature of 37.0 C on prior records. Today her temperature is 37.9 C with new lethargy. How should this be interpreted using age-adjusted fever thresholds?
choices: A fever by geriatric criteria, since it is nearly 1 C above her documented baseline and exceeds the single-reading threshold of 37.8 C
Not a fever, since 37.9 C is below the traditional adult threshold of 38.0 C
Only significant if it exceeds 39 C
Fever criteria are identical regardless of documented baseline
quiz.why: Geriatric fever criteria include a single oral reading above 37.8 C or an increase of 1.1 C above a documented baseline; this patient's value clears the absolute threshold and approaches the baseline-rise criterion, so it should be treated as a fever prompting further workup. Using the traditional 38.0 C adult cutoff would miss this, and requiring 39 C would delay recognition even further.

quiz.q: A 76-year-old presents after a low-speed motor vehicle collision with a systolic blood pressure of 106 mmHg and a heart rate of 88, findings that would not trigger trauma team activation in a 30-year-old. Why do these same numbers matter more here?
choices: They do not matter more; trauma triage criteria are identical across all adult ages
Age 65 and older lowers the systolic blood pressure threshold for hypotension to under 110, so this reading meets trauma triage criteria that a younger patient's would not
Heart rate is the only vital sign adjusted for age in trauma triage
These vitals only matter if the patient is on anticoagulation
quiz.why: Trauma triage criteria specifically lower the hypotension threshold to under 110 mmHg systolic for patients 65 and older, so a reading that looks unremarkable in a younger adult meets criteria for concern in this patient. This adjustment is not limited to patients on anticoagulants, and blood pressure, not only heart rate, is the specifically adjusted parameter here.

quiz.q: An 89-year-old with a UTI develops new inattention and disorganized speech over several hours, fluctuating between clear and confused. Her son says she was completely normal yesterday. Which CAM feature combination is met?
choices: Chronic gradual decline plus intact attention, consistent with dementia rather than delirium
Only inattention is present, which is insufficient for a CAM diagnosis
Acute fluctuating onset plus inattention, plus disorganized thinking, sufficient for a CAM-positive delirium diagnosis
The CAM requires a formal cognitive test score, not history alone
quiz.why: The CAM requires acute, fluctuating onset plus inattention, plus either disorganized thinking or altered consciousness; this vignette has all of the required elements (sudden onset, fluctuation, inattention, disorganized speech), making it CAM-positive for delirium. It does not fit dementia's gradual, non-fluctuating course, and the CAM is a structured bedside assessment, not solely a formal cognitive test score.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old is found on the floor by a home health aide with no witnesses and no memory of the event. Vital signs and glucose are normal, and there is a laceration from the fall. Beyond wound care, what workup addresses the 'why' of this fall?
choices: No further workup is needed once the laceration is repaired
A CT scan of the chest only
Referral to physical therapy alone, without further evaluation
Orthostatic vital signs, medication review, gait assessment, and an ECG given the unwitnessed nature of the event
quiz.why: An unwitnessed fall with no clear memory of the event raises concern for a possible syncopal or arrhythmic cause, so orthostatics, medication review, gait assessment, and an ECG are indicated in addition to treating the laceration. Wound care alone, chest CT without a clear indication, or physical therapy referral alone would all miss a potentially serious underlying cause.

quiz.q: A geriatric patient's medication list includes a benzodiazepine, an anticholinergic antihistamine, and an NSAID, totaling 7 regular medications. What does this list represent, and why does the count itself matter?
choices: Polypharmacy, defined as 5 or more regular medications, which independently raises the risk of adverse drug events beyond any single drug's risk
This does not qualify as polypharmacy since fewer than 10 medications are listed
A normal medication burden for this age group requiring no review
Polypharmacy only applies to patients on more than 15 medications
quiz.why: Polypharmacy is defined at 5 or more regular medications, and this list of 7, especially containing multiple Beers-flagged high-risk drugs, meets that definition and independently increases adverse drug event risk through interactions and cumulative burden. It is not a normal, unreviewed medication count at this age, and the threshold is well below 10 or 15.

quiz.q: An 85-year-old with dementia becomes newly agitated. Staff urge starting an antipsychotic right away. What should be evaluated first, consistent with avoiding a prescribing cascade?
choices: Start the antipsychotic immediately without further evaluation
Screen for a reversible cause such as pain, constipation, infection, or a new medication before adding another drug
Increase the dose of an existing sedative instead
Restrain the patient physically as the primary intervention
quiz.why: New agitation in dementia often has a reversible underlying cause (pain, constipation, infection, medication effect), and treating it directly with a new psychoactive drug without looking for that cause risks a prescribing cascade and unnecessary Beers-flagged medication exposure. Increasing an existing sedative or using restraint as a primary intervention does not address a potential underlying cause and carries its own risks.

quiz.q: A 90-year-old with end-stage heart failure wants to stay home, avoid hospitalization, and focus on comfort, with a life expectancy her cardiologist estimates at under 6 months. Which service best fits her stated goals?
choices: Palliative care alongside continued aggressive heart failure treatment
A POLST alone, without enrolling in any additional service
Hospice care, since she meets the prognosis criterion and wants to forgo further curative-intent treatment in favor of comfort
Long-term care placement, unrelated to her stated goals
quiz.why: With a prognosis of 6 months or less and a clear preference to forgo curative-intent treatment for comfort at home, hospice is the service that matches both her prognosis and her goals. Palliative care alongside aggressive treatment does not match her wish to stop curative measures, a POLST alone documents orders but is not itself a care program, and long-term care placement does not address her goal of staying home.
